_exec_summary.SummaryText:
Accidental Release Prevention and Emergency Response Policies 
FUJIFILM Wako Chemicals is committed to ensuring the safety of employees, the public, and the environment. The key components of this commitment include release prevention programs and emergency action planning. Health, safety, and environmental performance are embedded in corporate sustainability policy.  With a focus on Sustainability: we operate in a safe, ethically responsible, and environmentally sound manner in line with customer demands and community expectations. Numerous risk management practices are implemented to minimize hazards and ensure safe operations.
Stationary Source and Regulated Substances Handled 
FUJIFILM Wako Chemicals is a certified ISO 9001 chemical manufacturing site specializing in specialty chemicals. One chemical, Anhydrous hydrogen chloride (AHCl) used in manufacturing, FUJIFILM Wako Chemicals to have this EPA Risk Management Plan.
The AHCl is a liquid stored under pressure and vaporized for use in the manufacturing process. Two tube trailers (approximately 21,000 lbs. per trailer) are typically onsite. The maximum onsite capacity is 63,000 lbs.  (three trailers). Safety Controls for AHCl include over-pressuring and potential dangers are mitigated by control valves, rupture discs, relief valves, excess flow valves, close observation by plant personnel and only one tube is active at any time to reduce overall risk.
General Accidental Release Prevention Program and Chemical-Specific Prevention Steps 
To minimize accidental releases, FUJIFILM Wako employs the following layers of safety management system: well-trained employees operate with accurate SOPs and receive strong management and engineering support, comprehensive mechanical integrity including inspection and testing of equipment to reduce the likelihood of failures, regular hazard reviews identify potential risks for all processes involving hazardous materials, allowing preventive corrective actions, process control sy

stems maintain precise process control and tight operational parameters, and monitoring systems for early-warning detectors to immediately identify potential problems, enabling quick and effective responses.  
Five-Year Accident History 
There were no accidental releases that meet RMP reporting criteria since the last RMP submission (2019-2025).  
Emergency Action Planning 
As a non-responding facility, the Emergency Action Plan addresses responsibilities and actions for serious incidents (e.g., spills, releases, injuries). The plan goals are to protect employees, contractors, visitors, and facility assets and ensures compliance with EPA RMP requirements (40 CFR Part 68). In case of an accidental release, external responders are notified and provided detailed emergency plans.
In addition to training and conducting drills with those on-site, there is coordination with external responders to ensure active collaboration with fire departments, HAZMAT teams, and emergency medical services. Pre-emergency sharing of hazard information is done to improve coordinated responses.
As part of the pre-emergency planning, the Worst-Case Scenario and Alternate Release Scenario was completed to provide a comprehensive understanding of potential risks associated with anhydrous hydrogen chloride at the facility. By combining robust active mitigation systems with ongoing process safety improvements, the facility minimizes the risks of accidental releases and their impact on workers, the public, and the environment.
The Worst-Case Scenario:  The individually isolated tubes in the trailer represent the largest vessels containing HCl at the facility.  The largest single quantity of release was identified as a single filled tube containing up to 3500 lbs. of anhydrous HCl. Per Section 3.1.1 of the guidance, this was assumed to be released over 10 minutes because there is no passive mitigation in place. 
Alternate Release Scenario: much of the piping system downstream of the tube trailer is

protected by active mitigation consisting of a gas monitoring system which interlocks a valve. This stops the flow from the connected tube trailer in the event of a release. A section of piping containing a manual connection and transfer hose is located upstream of the shutoff valve. The Alternate Release Scenario chosen was failure of this connection, hose or section of tubing which are not mitigated by the interlock
Planned Changes to Improve Safety 
The Operational Improvement Project involves a cross-functional team (production, engineering, maintenance, quality, and EHS) working toward assessing current process and equipment conditions, prioritizing improvement projects, including capital investments, and improving SOPs and operator training. The projects goal is to reduce process variability, improve stability, enhance quality and safety, and minimize risk.
Planning an on-site drill involving Chesterfield County Emergency Response and Airgas. This drill will simulate a response to an HCL leak to improve readiness and coordination. An After-Action Review and Learning event will be conducted after the drill to identify improvements needed and share lessons learned with others.
